messages.content: I want to design a mixed-criticality accelerator runtime with a precise goal: under declared execution and interference bounds, every admitted control job must meet its 2 ms deadline. The runtime also has to guarantee starvation-free inference progress under adversarial arrivals, without compromising those admitted control deadlines. The difficult parts are nonpreemptible inference kernels and shared-memory interference.

That sets two obligations for the same runtime. The control guarantee is conditional on the declared execution and interference bounds and applies to *admitted* control jobs: each must finish by its 2 ms deadline. The inference guarantee rules out letting inference wait indefinitely merely because arrivals continue to compete for the accelerator. Neither obligation can be considered in isolation, because an inference kernel that cannot be preempted can delay control work, while shared-memory interference can affect how long work takes.
Can you clarify the scope of the 2 ms guarantee? I don't want it to sound like every control job is guaranteed a deadline regardless of load.

The scope is specifically **all admitted control jobs**, under the **declared execution and interference bounds**. Admission is therefore part of the guarantee's boundary: the statement does not promise that every arriving control job can be admitted. Nor does it assert a deadline guarantee when the declared bounds do not hold. Once a control job is admitted within those conditions, though, its 2 ms deadline is a requirement, not a best-effort target.
And why does nonpreemptibility matter if control work is more critical?

Criticality alone cannot interrupt a nonpreemptible inference kernel already running. A control job may have to wait for that kernel to finish before it can use the accelerator. So a deadline argument has to account for possible blocking by inference, rather than assuming control can always begin immediately. That is a general consequence of nonpreemptibility; it does not by itself specify which kernels the runtime should start or when.
Shared-memory interference is a separate issue, right? It isn't just another name for waiting behind a kernel.

Right. Waiting for a nonpreemptible kernel is one source of delay. Shared-memory interference concerns effects on execution while work contends for shared memory resources. The control deadline must hold with both kinds of effects accounted for under the declared bounds. Treating only the time spent waiting for the accelerator as the entire delay could miss interference during execution.
What should 'under declared execution and interference bounds' communicate here?

It makes the guarantee conditional and checkable in principle. The deadline claim relies on stated limits for relevant execution time and interference, rather than assuming either can grow without limit. Those limits must be sufficient to cover the effects that matter to an admitted control job, including any delay from nonpreemptible inference work. The goal does not provide numerical bounds for those effects, so it would be premature to present a particular timing calculation as established.
I also don't want 'inference progress' to quietly become 'inference gets whatever time is left if there happens to be any.' How do you read starvation-free under adversarial arrivals?

It is stronger than a hope that inference runs during occasional idle periods. Starvation-free progress means continuing arrivals must not be able to postpone waiting inference work forever. At the same time, the progress guarantee cannot be obtained by allowing an inference kernel to make an admitted control job miss its 2 ms deadline. The runtime's stated goal is to satisfy both properties together, even when arrival patterns are adversarial.
Does that require a fixed inference latency bound?

Not from the wording given. Starvation-free progress excludes indefinite postponement; it does not, by itself, specify a numerical response-time bound for inference. The only numerical deadline stated here is the 2 ms deadline for admitted control jobs. It is important not to replace the inference requirement with a stronger, unstated latency promise, or with a weaker promise of aggregate inference throughput that could leave particular waiting work starved.
What tension do adversarial arrivals introduce between those guarantees?

Arrivals can continue to create competition for accelerator time. If control work were admitted without regard to what its deadlines permit, or if inference could always be deferred in favor of newly arriving work, one of the obligations could be lost. Conversely, starting nonpreemptible inference work without accounting for the blocking it may impose could threaten an admitted control deadline. The design problem is to make the admission and execution choices compatible with both guarantees; this statement does not yet prescribe a particular policy for doing so.
Suppose someone says, 'Just always prioritize control.' Would that fully express the goal?

No. Prioritizing control does not remove blocking from an inference kernel that has already begun and cannot be preempted. It also does not, on its own, establish starvation-free inference progress under adversarial arrivals: a stream of higher-priority arrivals could keep inference waiting. Priority may be a scheduling concept, but simply naming it would not prove either of the two stated guarantees.
And 'just let inference run sometimes' sounds too weak in the other direction.

Yes. Occasional inference execution would not necessarily show that waiting inference work cannot starve. It would also need to be compatible with the 2 ms deadlines of admitted control jobs, taking nonpreemptible execution and shared-memory interference into account. The goal is a guarantee about behavior under the stated conditions, not merely an intention to give both classes some attention.
Can we state the design target without implying that the runtime or its proof already exists?

The target is to design a mixed-criticality accelerator runtime that accounts for nonpreemptible inference kernels and shared-memory interference, guarantees that all admitted control jobs meet their 2 ms deadlines under declared execution and interference bounds, and guarantees starvation-free inference progress under adversarial arrivals without sacrificing those control deadlines. That is a specification to meet, not a claim that a particular implementation or analysis has already met it.
So the word 'admitted' limits the control obligation, but it shouldn't become an escape hatch for never serving inference.

Exactly. Restricting the deadline guarantee to admitted control jobs does not erase the separate inference-progress requirement. A design that protects control deadlines only by postponing inference forever would fail the stated goal. Likewise, making inference progress by violating an admitted control job's 2 ms deadline would fail it. Both obligations have to hold simultaneously within the declared execution and interference bounds.
I'd also like to keep clear that shared-memory effects cannot simply be ignored when checking a control deadline.

They cannot be ignored: the condition explicitly includes declared interference bounds. A control job's ability to meet its 2 ms deadline has to be assessed with the relevant shared-memory interference accounted for, alongside execution and any blocking from nonpreemptible inference kernels. Otherwise the claimed deadline guarantee would not address one of the stated challenges.
Is there any specific arrival pattern, kernel length, or interference magnitude I should assume from this goal?

No specific pattern, kernel length, or interference magnitude is supplied. 'Adversarial arrivals' says the inference-progress guarantee must withstand unfavorable arrivals, while the control guarantee is conditioned on declared execution and interference bounds. The goal does not give values for those bounds or choose an implementation mechanism. Keeping those details open preserves the distinction between the required guarantees and the design that would establish them.

For the runtime design, I propose admitting control jobs against 2-ms response bounds. Those bounds would account for reserved FIFO inference slots, bounded nonpreemptible inference kernels, and shared-memory interference.

That makes admission conditional on a response-time argument rather than on a preference for control work. A control job would be admitted only if its bound, including the effects you named, fits within 2 ms. The proposal treats reserved FIFO inference slots as part of the time control work may have to wait, and it also accounts for nonpreemptible kernel execution and shared-memory interference.
I want to be clear about the admission test. Is it a prediction of typical response time?

No. A typical or average response time would not establish the stated deadline guarantee. The proposed test is against a **response bound**: under the declared execution and interference bounds, admission must be justified by an upper bound of no more than 2 ms for the control job. The proposal does not specify how to calculate that bound, but it does specify effects that the calculation cannot omit.
Why include reserved inference slots in a control-job response bound? Aren't those slots meant for inference?

Precisely because they are meant for inference. If inference has reserved opportunities to run, a control response bound cannot silently assume that all accelerator time is available to control. It needs to allow for whatever delay those reserved FIFO inference slots can impose on a control job, while still fitting that job's response within 2 ms. The proposal does not state a slot duration or reservation frequency.
Does FIFO describe control admission, or is it attached to the inference slots?

Here it is attached to the **reserved inference slots**: the proposal calls them reserved FIFO inference slots. It does not say that control jobs themselves are admitted in FIFO order, nor does it specify an overall scheduling order beyond that phrase. Any more detailed interpretation of the queueing or slot mechanism would need additional information.
What does the bounded-kernel part add if the bound already accounts for the slots?

A reservation and a nonpreemptible kernel describe different considerations. The reservation represents inference execution opportunities that the response argument must respect. A nonpreemptible kernel, once running, cannot be interrupted just because control work needs the accelerator, so its bounded execution can contribute blocking. The response bound must account for the relevant effects without assuming that a slot boundary instantly stops a kernel.
So the kernel cannot simply be treated as preemptible at the point a control job arrives?

Correct. The proposal explicitly accounts for **bounded nonpreemptible kernels**. An admission argument that relies on interrupting one immediately would not address that condition. The bounded part is what makes its possible delay something a response-bound analysis can incorporate; no numerical kernel bound is specified here.
And the shared-memory interference should be inside the same response argument, not left as an informal caveat?

Yes. Shared-memory interference is one of the effects the proposed 2-ms response bounds must account for. Leaving it outside the bound while still claiming the bound covers the job's response would understate what the admission test is meant to consider. The proposal does not quantify that interference or prescribe a particular way to model it.
Would it be accurate to say that admission passes whenever a control job's bounded response is exactly 2 ms?

As a statement about the proposed threshold, a bound of **no more than 2 ms** fits a 2-ms deadline, including equality, provided the bound really covers the relevant execution, reservation, nonpreemptible blocking, and shared-memory interference under the declared conditions. This does not tell us whether any particular job has such a bound; no job-specific values have been given.
Suppose there is room for a control job's own execution, but not after the reserved inference opportunity is considered. Would the proposal still admit it?

No, not on that incomplete reasoning. The proposed admission test is against the control job's **response** bound, not just its own execution time. If accounting for the reserved FIFO inference slots causes that response bound to exceed 2 ms, the proposed criterion would not justify admitting the job. The same principle applies to the bounded nonpreemptible-kernel effects and shared-memory interference.
Does this proposal already establish that inference cannot starve under adversarial arrivals?

It includes reserved FIFO inference slots, which gives the admission argument a way to respect inference opportunities instead of assuming control can consume all available time. But the proposal alone does not specify enough about how those opportunities recur or how waiting inference work receives them to establish starvation-free progress under adversarial arrivals. That remains a requirement of the runtime design, not a result to infer solely from the words 'reserved FIFO inference slots.'
Similarly, does saying '2-ms response bounds' mean we have already proved every admitted control deadline?

Not by itself. It states the proposed basis for admission: control jobs are admitted against bounds that must account for the listed sources of delay. To support the deadline guarantee, the bounds would have to be valid under the declared execution and interference conditions, and admission would have to apply them as intended. The node proposes that approach; it does not report completed bounds or measured deadline outcomes.
I'm trying to distinguish a control job's deadline from the maximum length of an inference kernel. Both sound like time limits.

They have different roles. **2 ms** is the response-time threshold against which a control job is admitted. A bound on a nonpreemptible inference kernel limits how long that kind of kernel can block other work once it is running. The proposal supplies the 2-ms figure but does not supply a numerical kernel-duration bound. The kernel bound is an input to the response argument, not a replacement for the control deadline.
Should I read the proposal as reserving inference time regardless of whether doing so would break an admitted control deadline?

No. The proposal specifically requires control admission against response bounds that account for the reserved inference slots. The intended compatibility is that a control job is admitted only when its 2-ms response bound still holds with those slots included. It does not authorize disregarding an admitted deadline when an inference slot comes up.
Conversely, could an admission analysis ignore inference reservations to make more control jobs appear admissible?

That would contradict this proposal. The reserved FIFO inference slots are explicitly among the effects included in the 2-ms response bounds. Excluding them could make a control job appear to have a shorter response bound than the proposed design actually permits. The point is to assess admission against the work the runtime is intended to accommodate, not against an imagined inference-free accelerator.
Can you restate the proposal without adding an algorithm or a numerical interference assumption?

Admit control jobs only against 2-ms response bounds that account for reserved FIFO inference slots, bounded nonpreemptible inference kernels, and shared-memory interference. That states the admission principle and its required accounting. It leaves the exact bound calculation, slot configuration, kernel limits, and interference limits unspecified.
One last distinction: if those effects are individually bounded, can I automatically add their worst cases and announce a valid control response bound?

Their individual boundedness makes a response-bound argument possible, but this proposal does not specify a formula or establish that any particular combination is valid. The analysis must correctly represent how the reserved FIFO inference slots, nonpreemptible kernels, and shared-memory interference affect a control job's response under the declared bounds. Only then could the resulting bound be compared with 2 ms for admission.
What positive inference-slot reservation preserves 2-ms control response bounds under worst-case arrivals and shared-memory interference?

That is the key sizing question, but the information so far does not determine a numerical reservation. A candidate must reserve a nonzero opportunity for inference while keeping every admitted control job's worst-case response bound at or below 2 ms. That bound must include the reservation's effect, blocking by bounded nonpreemptible inference kernels, and shared-memory interference under the declared bounds.
By positive, I mean inference should have an actual reserved opportunity, not a reservation of zero that makes the control analysis easy.

Yes. Zero would avoid delay attributable to a reservation, but it would not answer the question. The question asks whether some *strictly positive* inference-slot reservation can coexist with the 2-ms response bounds, and, if so, which one. A reservation cannot be called suitable solely because it helps inference; it must also be included in the control response analysis.
Could we answer 'use the smallest positive slot'?

Not without defining what a slot reserves and how it recurs. A very short opportunity might have little effect on a control bound, but that observation does not establish inference progress, especially when inference kernels are nonpreemptible. Nor does 'smallest positive' identify a value when no minimum slot size, kernel bound, or reservation schedule has been specified.
What is it about worst-case arrivals that makes the question harder than checking an otherwise idle accelerator?

An idle-period check would omit the contention the question explicitly asks about. Under worst-case arrivals, a control job could encounter the unfavorable timing of reserved inference opportunities and nonpreemptible inference execution while other admitted work also needs service. The response argument has to cover the arrival patterns allowed by its declared assumptions, rather than relying on a convenient gap in demand.
I don't want 'worst case' to be interpreted as unlimited control work with no admission condition.

That distinction matters. The 2-ms guarantee is for *admitted* control jobs under declared bounds. Asking for robustness to worst-case arrivals means considering the most adverse arrivals covered by those conditions; it does not silently promise to admit an unlimited number of control jobs and meet all their deadlines. If the permitted arrival conditions are not specified, we cannot calculate how much reservation they leave feasible.
How should shared-memory interference enter this reservation question?

It belongs in the worst-case response bound used to evaluate a candidate reservation. A slot that appears compatible with 2 ms when considering accelerator occupancy alone might not be compatible once the declared shared-memory interference is included. The question therefore asks about a reservation that preserves the bound *with* interference accounted for, not one that works only if interference happens to be absent.
Is interference necessarily caused by the inference slot itself?

The question does not establish a particular cause or amount of interference. It says that shared-memory interference must be considered when assessing whether a positive inference-slot reservation preserves the control bounds. It would be unwarranted to equate all interference with the slot, or to assume the slot has no interaction with it, without further information.
What role do nonpreemptible kernels play when deciding how much to reserve?

They prevent us from treating a reserved opportunity as though inference could always stop instantaneously when control needs the accelerator. The relevant bounded nonpreemptible execution has to be reflected in a control job's worst-case response. A proposed reservation is acceptable only if the response analysis remains within 2 ms after accounting for that possible blocking as well as the reservation and shared-memory interference.
Could a positive reservation be feasible for some admitted control workload but not for another?

In principle, yes: whether a candidate fits a 2-ms response bound depends on the admitted jobs and the declared execution, arrival, and interference conditions being analyzed. That is why the question cannot be answered with a universal slot size from the information given. The reservation has to be evaluated against the particular bounds that define the admission guarantee, without assuming a workload that has not been stated.
Would 'reserve whatever time remains after control' count as an answer?

Not necessarily. Under unfavorable arrivals there may be no opportunistic remainder, so that wording alone does not identify a *positive reserved* inference opportunity. The question is about an explicit nonzero reservation whose effect is already accommodated in admitted control jobs' 2-ms response bounds. It does not ask merely whether inference could run when the accelerator happens to be free.
I also don't want to assume that any positive fraction automatically prevents inference starvation.

That caution is warranted. A positive reservation is relevant to inference progress, but the amount of reserved time alone does not establish how waiting inference work obtains service or whether nonpreemptible kernels can make progress through the available opportunities. The present question is narrower: identify a positive inference-slot reservation that remains compatible with the control response bounds under the stated worst-case conditions.
Is the answer simply 'make the slots FIFO'?

FIFO describes an ordering associated with the reserved inference slots in the proposal; it does not give their size or timing. Ordering alone cannot show that an admitted control job's worst-case response stays within 2 ms. To answer the reservation question, one would still need to account for how those opportunities delay control, including nonpreemptible execution and shared-memory interference.
Suppose a candidate reservation just fits the 2-ms bound when interference is ignored. Can it be called safe?

No, not on that basis. The question expressly requires preserving the bounds under shared-memory interference. If a candidate reaches 2 ms before that effect is included, it has not been shown to meet the required bound under the declared interference conditions. We cannot infer the final result without the interference bound and a valid response analysis.
Does 'preserves 2-ms control response bounds' mean the response bound has to stay strictly below 2 ms?

The stated deadline is 2 ms, so a valid worst-case response bound of no more than 2 ms would meet that threshold; strict inequality is not specified. The strict condition in the question is on the inference reservation: it must be *positive*. Whether a candidate yields a response bound below or exactly at 2 ms cannot be determined from the information supplied.
What would you need to know before naming a reservation rather than just describing the test?

At minimum, the response analysis would need the declared bounds governing control execution and admissible arrivals, the relevant bound on nonpreemptible inference kernels, the shared-memory interference bound, and a definition of what the reserved inference slots provide and when. Without those, naming a slot length, rate, or fraction would introduce a value unsupported by the question.
Could the honest outcome of the analysis be that no positive reservation fits?

Yes, that is a possible outcome of the *question*, not an outcome established here. If every candidate positive reservation caused some admitted control response bound to exceed 2 ms under the declared worst-case conditions, then none would meet this criterion for those conditions. Conversely, a candidate shown to keep all relevant bounds at or below 2 ms would meet the control side of the criterion. We have neither calculation.
So how would you phrase the open issue in one sentence without pretending we have solved it?

Determine whether a strictly positive reserved FIFO inference-slot opportunity can be chosen so that, under worst-case arrivals and the declared execution and shared-memory interference bounds, every admitted control job's response bound—including reservation effects and bounded nonpreemptible inference blocking—remains no more than 2 ms.
Does framing it that way keep the inference and control concerns connected?

Yes. The reservation is positive so inference is not excluded from the design, while the 2-ms bound constrains how that reservation may affect admitted control jobs. The question remains open until the reservation and the relevant worst-case bounds are specified and evaluated; it does not itself claim that a compatible reservation has been found.

Here's a concrete hypothesis for the reservation: reserve 200 µs every 8 ms for FIFO inference kernels of at most 200 µs. With interference-aware control admission, I think this could preserve 2-ms control deadlines and inference progress.

That gives the open reservation question a specific candidate: a 200-µs inference opportunity every 8 ms, for kernels bounded at 200 µs and served FIFO. The proposed deadline claim still depends on interference-aware admission showing that every admitted control job has a response bound of no more than 2 ms with that reservation included. The inference-progress claim is also part of the hypothesis, not an established result.
I want the two time values to remain distinct. What does each one specify?

The **200 µs** is the length of the proposed reserved inference slot and the stated upper bound on an individual FIFO inference kernel. The **8 ms** is the interval at which the 200-µs reservation recurs. Neither value changes the separate **2 ms** deadline for admitted control jobs.
So this isn't proposing 200 µs of inference time in every 2-ms control window?

Correct. The hypothesis says **200 µs every 8 ms**, not 200 µs every 2 ms. A control response analysis must nevertheless consider where a job's 2-ms response interval could fall relative to a reserved slot. It cannot assume the slot is harmless merely because its recurrence interval is longer than the control deadline.
Why pair a 200-µs slot with kernels bounded at 200 µs?

The pairing proposes that an eligible nonpreemptible kernel is no longer than the reserved opportunity. That is relevant to making reserved slots useful for inference while limiting the blocking control work might encounter. It is not, by itself, proof that every such kernel fits in the slot under shared-memory interference; the meaning and validity of the kernel bound must be consistent with the interference-aware analysis.
Would it be fair to call this a positive reservation rather than leftover capacity?

Yes. Reserving 200 µs every 8 ms specifies a recurring, nonzero inference opportunity. It is different from saying inference may run only when control work leaves spare time. Whether this particular positive reservation is compatible with all admitted control jobs' 2-ms bounds is what the hypothesis still needs to establish.
The arithmetic works out to 2.5% of the 8-ms interval. Is that a useful way to describe it?

As a description of the nominal reservation, yes: 200 µs divided by 8 ms is 2.5%. That ratio does not itself establish either guarantee. Control deadlines depend on worst-case timing and interference, not just the average reserved share, and inference progress depends on usable recurring service for waiting FIFO kernels.
Can you explain why a small average share might still matter to a 2-ms control response?

A response bound concerns the delay a particular job can experience at an unfavorable time, not merely average accelerator occupancy. If a control job encounters a reserved inference slot or a nonpreemptible kernel, the resulting delay has to fit in its 2-ms bound along with its other accounted-for execution and interference. The 2.5% nominal share alone says nothing about that worst-case alignment.
Where exactly does interference-aware admission enter the hypothesis?

It is the proposed safeguard for the control side: admission should accept a control job only when its 2-ms response bound remains valid after accounting for the 200-µs-every-8-ms reservation, bounded nonpreemptible inference execution, and declared shared-memory interference. The hypothesis gives no interference magnitude or completed response calculation, so it does not yet show which jobs would be admitted.
I don't mean that merely setting a 200-µs kernel limit proves the interference is bounded appropriately.

Right. A stated kernel limit and an interference bound have to be interpreted consistently. If shared-memory interference can affect how long a kernel runs or how long a control job takes, the admission argument cannot silently ignore that effect when using the ≤200-µs kernel condition or checking the 2-ms deadline. The hypothesis does not specify how those bounds are established.
Does FIFO matter to the deadline analysis as well as to inference progress?

The reservation and bounded nonpreemptible kernels matter directly to possible control blocking, and the proposed FIFO service describes the order in which inference kernels use their opportunities. FIFO is especially relevant to the progress claim because later inference arrivals should not continually pass earlier waiting kernels. But FIFO alone does not quantify a control response bound; the timing of reserved execution and interference still need to be accounted for.
Could I say the 200-µs slot guarantees a kernel completes every 8 ms?

That would be stronger than the hypothesis establishes. It proposes a recurring slot for FIFO kernels of at most 200 µs, but it does not specify enough about slot usability, queued work, or the treatment of interference to announce a completed-kernel count for each 8-ms interval. The defensible statement is that this arrangement is hypothesized to preserve inference progress.
What if adversarial inference arrivals keep coming? Why would FIFO be helpful?

FIFO prevents newly arriving inference kernels from overtaking a kernel already waiting ahead of them, which is relevant when arrivals are adversarial. Coupled with recurring usable reserved opportunities and the stated kernel bound, that gives a plausible route to starvation-free progress. The hypothesis does not supply a proof that those opportunities provide the needed service under all arrivals covered by the goal, so this remains a proposed argument rather than a demonstrated guarantee.
And adversarial control arrivals shouldn't be treated as a reason to cancel the reservation whenever convenient, should they?

Not if the reservation is to support the stated inference-progress hypothesis. Its effect should instead be included when deciding whether control jobs can be admitted with 2-ms response bounds under the declared conditions. That keeps the control guarantee tied to admission and the inference opportunity tied to an actual positive reservation, rather than making either depend on an unexpectedly quiet arrival pattern.
Could this hypothesis preserve deadlines by admitting no control jobs at all?

An empty admitted set would make a statement about admitted control deadlines vacuous, but it would not demonstrate a useful mixed-criticality design. The hypothesis does not state an admission rate or guarantee that any particular arriving control job is admitted. The substantive test is whether interference-aware admission can admit the intended control work while maintaining valid 2-ms bounds alongside the proposed inference reservation; no such workload has been specified here.
I also don't want to turn inference progress into a fixed inference deadline.

The hypothesis does not assign inference jobs a numerical deadline. The 8-ms figure describes how often a 200-µs slot is reserved, not a promise that every inference job finishes within 8 ms. The proposed inference property is progress, with FIFO and recurring reserved opportunities intended to prevent indefinite postponement; the only stated job deadline remains 2 ms for admitted control jobs.
Could we already conclude that the 200-µs reservation is the right answer to the sizing question?

Not yet. It is a concrete **hypothesized answer** to evaluate. To conclude that it works, the control response bounds would need to remain within 2 ms under the relevant worst-case arrivals and shared-memory interference, including any nonpreemptible blocking. The inference side would also need to show that FIFO kernels make starvation-free progress with the reserved opportunities. Neither result is supplied by the proposed numbers alone.
What is the most concise accurate statement of the hypothesis?

Hypothesis: reserving **200 µs every 8 ms** for **FIFO inference kernels bounded at 200 µs**, while admitting control jobs using **interference-aware 2-ms response bounds**, preserves admitted control deadlines and inference progress. It states the candidate and the claimed properties without presenting either property as already proved.
If the interference-aware bound for a control job exceeded 2 ms with this reservation, would this proposal tell us to admit it anyway for the sake of inference?

No. Interference-aware admission is part of the hypothesis precisely so that a job whose accounted-for response exceeds 2 ms would not be admitted on a claim that its 2-ms deadline is protected. The proposal aims to preserve inference progress *without compromising admitted control deadlines*. It does not say that a positive inference reservation overrides the control admission criterion.
And if a control bound fits only by pretending the inference slot won't occur during the job's response?

That would not support this hypothesis unless the declared timing conditions genuinely exclude the slot from that response. Otherwise the bound must account for the unfavorable placement of the 200-µs reservation, as well as bounded nonpreemptible kernel effects and shared-memory interference. A claimed 2-ms response bound that omits a possible reserved-slot delay would not test the candidate being proposed.
So at this stage we're putting forward exact reservation and kernel figures, but not claiming an evaluated worst-case bound?

Exactly. The candidate is specific—**200 µs every 8 ms**, with **≤200-µs FIFO inference kernels** and interference-aware control admission—but its two outcomes remain hypothesized. The exact figures identify what should be assessed; they do not substitute for showing that admitted control responses stay within 2 ms and that inference continues to progress under adversarial arrivals.
The next step I want to plan is to derive interference-aware 2-ms control-response bounds and FIFO inference-service bounds for 200-µs slots every 8 ms under adversarial arrivals.

That plan calls for two connected analyses. The control-response bound must account for the recurring 200-µs reservation, nonpreemptible execution, and shared-memory interference when checking whether an admitted control job can meet its 2-ms deadline. The FIFO service bound must describe what service waiting inference work can obtain from those slots even when arrivals are adversarial. These are bounds to derive, not results already calculated.
Why derive both bounds together rather than just a control-response bound?

The control bound addresses whether reserving the slots is compatible with admitted control deadlines. It does not, on its own, say what waiting inference kernels receive. The FIFO service bound addresses that other side of the design: whether the reserved opportunities yield inference progress despite adversarial arrivals. Both analyses need to describe the same 200-µs-every-8-ms reservation consistently.
What should the 2-ms control-response derivation actually cover?

It should bound a control job's response under the declared execution and interference conditions, allowing for unfavorable arrival timing relative to the reserved slots and for any relevant blocking from nonpreemptible inference kernels. The resulting bound is what interference-aware admission would compare with 2 ms. The plan does not provide a formula or the values needed to evaluate one.
So it cannot just subtract the average reservation share from accelerator capacity?

Not as a complete response-time argument. A job's 2-ms response can depend on when it arrives relative to a slot, not only on the average share reserved over 8 ms. The derivation needs to cover the worst-case timing allowed by its assumptions, together with shared-memory interference. A capacity average may describe the reservation, but it does not replace a response bound.
Does the 8-ms recurrence make it safe to assume a 2-ms control response never encounters a slot?

No. A 2-ms interval can overlap a 200-µs slot even though slots recur every 8 ms. The planned bound has to consider an unfavorable alignment rather than assuming control work always arrives between reserved opportunities. Exactly how the overlap affects a response depends on the timing and execution conditions the derivation uses.
And the shared-memory interference belongs in the derivation itself?

Yes. The planned control bound is explicitly **interference-aware**. It should reflect the declared shared-memory interference rather than checking 2 ms under interference-free execution and attaching a separate caveat afterward. The plan does not specify an interference magnitude or model, so it cannot yet produce a numerical response bound.
What does adversarial arrival timing mean for the control side? I don't want to imply unlimited jobs are admitted.

The derivation should handle adverse arrivals within the conditions used for admission. It need not—and the goal does not—promise 2-ms deadlines for an unlimited set of control arrivals regardless of admission. The control statement remains about jobs that are admitted using valid response bounds under the declared conditions.
Where does nonpreemptibility enter, given that this plan names slots and FIFO service rather than a new kernel mechanism?

It remains a timing effect the control-response derivation cannot wish away. A kernel already running cannot be assumed to stop immediately when a control job arrives. The analysis has to account for the relevant bounded nonpreemptible execution when assessing the effect of the reserved inference opportunities. This plan does not change how kernels execute.
On the inference side, what would a FIFO service bound describe?

It would characterize the service available to waiting inference kernels through the recurring 200-µs slots, taking FIFO order and adversarial arrivals into account. In particular, it should support reasoning about whether later arrivals can indefinitely delay work already waiting. That is distinct from assigning every inference job a fixed deadline; none is stated here.
If arrivals keep coming, could a FIFO bound rely on a future quiet period?

It should not if it is intended to address adversarial arrivals. A bound that works only when arrivals stop would not address the stated condition. FIFO order is relevant because new arrivals do not move ahead of earlier waiting work, but the derivation must also account for whether the reserved slots provide usable service. FIFO ordering alone is not a service bound.
Could we claim one inference kernel finishes in each 8-ms interval as the FIFO bound?

The plan does not establish that claim. A 200-µs slot every 8 ms specifies a reservation, but a completed-kernel count also depends on how execution fits the slot under the declared conditions, including relevant interference. The purpose of deriving the FIFO service bound is to determine what can actually be guaranteed, rather than assuming a completion rate from the slot dimensions alone.
Would the FIFO service bound necessarily give every inference kernel the same waiting-time limit?

Not necessarily. A kernel's wait can depend on how much work is already ahead of it in FIFO order. The stated plan is to derive service bounds under adversarial arrivals, not to assert a single numerical inference deadline. No. The activity calls for testing **200 µs of execution** and **80 µs of DRAM stalls** as separate limits. In the stated kernel-plus-stall accounting, their sum is **280 µs**. What should 'configure DRAM QoS' mean here without presuming a particular hardware feature works?

And 'tiled kernels' shouldn't sound like we can interrupt a running tile at will.

Correct. Tiling identifies the kernel form to configure and test against the **200-µs execution limit**. It does not, by itself, make a running kernel preemptible. The relevant execution unit still needs to satisfy its bound without relying on interruption that the runtime cannot perform.
Could we admit a kernel merely because its tile is small in a source-level sense?

Not on that description alone. The check concerns **execution time: at most 200 µs** under the conditions being tested. Does adversarial contention apply only to the DRAM-stall test?

It applies to the testing activity as a whole. Contention can challenge the **80-µs stall limit** and the timing assumptions used when assessing a tiled kernel's **200-µs execution limit**. Why put these tests before admission rather than admit first and see how the jobs behave?

Admission depends on the declared timing limits being applicable to the work it accepts. If a candidate kernel or contention condition has not been checked against the **200-µs execution** and **80-µs stall** limits, admitting it on the assumption that those limits hold would leave the response argument unsupported. The activity therefore places the checks before admission, not after a possible timing violation.
Would a single favorable run with a stall below 80 µs settle the issue?

No. The stated test is under **adversarial contention**. A favorable observation can show what happened in that run but cannot establish that the stall will stay within **80 µs** under all permitted contention. The test must be interpreted with that limitation; no test outcome is stated here.
What if the measured execution is under 200 µs but the DRAM stall exceeds 80 µs?

Then the two-limit check has not passed: satisfying the execution limit would not compensate for violating the stall limit. Work could not be admitted *on the basis of both stated limits* under that condition. This is how to apply the proposed check, not a report that such a violation has occurred.
And if the stall is under 80 µs but execution exceeds 200 µs?

The converse applies. Meeting the **80-µs stall limit** does not establish the **200-µs execution limit**. Both are conditions to check before admission; the activity does not state that either has been met.
Does the sum of the limits mean that a kernel may always occupy exactly 280 µs?

No. **200 µs + 80 µs = 280 µs** is the upper-limit accounting when both contributions apply as separate terms. It is not a claim that every kernel uses the full execution and stall allowances, or that any test has recorded a 280-µs occupation. How those terms are measured must remain consistent with the admission and slot accounting.
Should we also check that the QoS configuration holds up when other work contends for DRAM, rather than testing a tiled kernel alone?

Yes—that is the point of testing **adversarial contention**. A standalone kernel timing check would not exercise the shared-memory interference relevant to the **80-µs DRAM-stall limit**. The activity calls for checking the configured QoS and tiled kernels under contention before relying on their limits for admission; it supplies no specific competing workload or test result.
Can these tests, by themselves, prove the limits for every possible adversarial pattern?

Finite tests can challenge the limits and expose violations, but passing tested patterns alone does not prove a universal worst-case guarantee. The admission argument still needs the limits to be justified for the declared operating conditions. This activity specifies configuration and pre-admission testing; it does not claim that the tests have established universal enforcement.
How does this relate to the 280-µs reserved FIFO slot without changing the slot policy?

The **200-µs execution** and **80-µs stall** limits are the components being tested for work that would rely on the **280-µs** timing allowance. This activity does not select a different slot length or recurrence interval. Its concern is whether the configured DRAM QoS and tiled kernels meet the limits used in admission and slot accounting under adversarial contention.
I don't want the inference-kernel check to be confused with control admission. Are they the same check?

They are related but distinct. Testing a tiled kernel against **200 µs of execution** and **80 µs of stalls** checks whether those assumptions can be used for that work. Control admission still has to account for blocking and shared-memory interference when assessing the admitted control job's **2-ms** deadline. Passing a kernel timing check alone does not automatically admit a control job.
Should DRAM QoS be described as already enforcing the 80-µs limit?

No. The activity says to **configure** DRAM QoS and **test** adversarial contention against the limit. It does not report that the configuration succeeded or that the hardware guarantees an 80-µs maximum. Those would be outcomes requiring evidence beyond the activity as stated.
What about saying tiled kernels have already met the 200-µs execution limit?

That would likewise turn a test objective into a result. The activity calls for configuring tiled kernels and testing them against **200 µs** before admission. It does not provide observed execution times or a completed timing certificate.
Can you restate the activity concisely without implying that we have selected tile sizes, run tests, or admitted jobs?

Configure **DRAM QoS and tiled kernels**, then test them under **adversarial contention** against separate limits of **200 µs of execution** and **80 µs of DRAM stalls** before admitting work on those assumptions. The configuration details, test results, and admission outcomes are not specified.
What did QoSStress-1 record for the tiled kernels under adversarial contention?

Does 'peaked' mean those are average times?
No. A peak is the highest recorded value for the stated measure in those launches. The evidence does not give an average execution time or an average DRAM stall time.
Are execution and DRAM stalls reported as separate measurements?
Yes. QoSStress-1 reports a **198-µs execution peak** and a **76-µs DRAM-stall peak**. Keeping the labels attached to their values matters; neither number is described as the other's measurement.
Can I say a single launch experienced both peaks?

Then adding 198 and 76 would be arithmetic on the reported peaks, not an observed per-launch total?

Exactly. Their arithmetic sum is **274 µs**, but the report does not say a launch had 198 µs of execution and 76 µs of stalls together. Nor does it state a separately measured peak for their combined duration. That distinction should remain explicit if the figures are discussed together.
Does 'one million launches' tell us how many different tiled kernels were involved?
No. It states the number of launches in QoSStress-1, not the number of distinct kernels, tiles, or configurations. No breakdown of that kind is supplied.
What does the adversarial-contention condition add to the finding?

It identifies the conditions under which these peaks were recorded: the launches were tested with adversarial contention, rather than described as isolated, contention-free executions. The finding does not specify the contending work or claim that every possible contention pattern was exercised.
Could I turn the million launches into a guarantee about every future launch?

No. A million recorded launches provide observations over that test set. Even under adversarial contention, finite observations do not alone establish a universal worst-case limit for every future launch or every permitted environment. The precise claim here is what QoSStress-1 recorded.
Does the evidence give a probability that execution or stalls exceed these peaks later?
No. It supplies observed maxima and the launch count, but no probability model, confidence interval, or estimate of future exceedance. The peaks should not be recast as statistical guarantees.
I also don't want 'adversarial' to become shorthand for exhaustive testing.

That's an important distinction. **Adversarial contention** describes the test condition reported for QoSStress-1; it does not mean that the million launches enumerate every possible arrival, memory-contention, or execution scenario. The evidence is specific about the observed peaks, not exhaustive coverage.
Should we describe the 198-µs figure as an end-to-end response time?

No. It is labeled **tiled-kernel execution**, not an end-to-end control response or inference waiting time. Likewise, **76 µs** is labeled DRAM stall time. The report does not provide a job response-time measurement.
And can we infer the FIFO queue's progress from these two peaks?

Not directly. QoSStress-1 reports execution and stall peaks for tiled-kernel launches under contention. It does not report FIFO queue order, backlog duration, or completion frequency. Those would be different observations from the two timing peaks stated here.
Does this report say what DRAM QoS settings were used?

No specific settings are given in the reported evidence. Naming QoSStress-1 does not supply a QoS parameter value, hardware model, or isolation mechanism. We should not invent any of those details to explain the recorded peaks.
Can we claim the tiled kernels were nonpreemptible throughout the measured launches?

This result calls them tiled kernels and reports their execution and stall peaks; it does not describe a per-launch preemption trace. Their role in the runtime's nonpreemptible-kernel accounting is context, but the QoSStress-1 finding itself does not add observations about when an individual launch could be interrupted.
How would you word the result so nobody reads 'peak' as an absolute hardware ceiling?

Say **'In QoSStress-1's one million launches under adversarial contention, the highest recorded tiled-kernel execution time was 198 µs, and the highest recorded DRAM stall time was 76 µs.'** The phrase 'highest recorded' keeps the scope tied to the test observations rather than asserting a hardware-enforced ceiling.
If someone asks whether the two figures were obtained under the same contention condition, what can we say?

Both are reported for QoSStress-1's launches **under adversarial contention**. That shared description does not tell us whether their individual peaks occurred on the same launch or under identical moment-by-moment contention. We can preserve the common test condition without adding that finer detail.
Does 'million launches' mean a million completions?

The evidence specifically says **one million launches**. It does not separately report a completion count, so the safest wording retains 'launches' rather than silently replacing it with a different metric.
What's the shortest faithful statement of the observation?

**QoSStress-1 recorded, across one million tiled-kernel launches under adversarial contention, peaks of 198 µs for execution and 76 µs for DRAM stalls.** These are observed peaks, not universal timing guarantees.

I don't want 'QoS-isolated' to sound like we've already proved that DRAM interference can never exceed its bound.

If the observed QoSStress-1 values were within those limits, why isn't that already enough?

And what role do the SlotGuard traces play in the decision?

They supply the other stated reason for conditional adoption: the SlotGuard traces **met the deadlines**. That is evidence about the replayed behavior under those traces. Can we say QoSStress-1 certified the kernels?

No. The decision expressly says to **require certified bounds before admission**, while citing QoSStress-1 for having stayed within the bounds during its test. Calling the test itself certification would collapse the distinction the decision makes. No completed certification is stated.
Does 'before admission' apply only to inference kernels, or can control work rely on uncertified bounds?

The gate applies wherever admission relies on these execution and interference bounds. A control job's deadline accounting can depend on the blocking and shared-memory behavior of admitted inference work, so uncertified assumptions about that work cannot safely be treated as established merely because the job being admitted is control work. The decision does not define separate certification procedures for the two classes.
Could the admission check accept a tiled kernel whose typical execution fits, even if its bound isn't certified?

Not under this decision. A typical time or a favorable test observation is not the **certified bound** required before admission. The condition is about the limit admission is allowed to rely on, not just whether a kernel usually appears to fit.
I'm also trying to avoid claiming the tests were hardware deployment results.

Nothing in this decision says SlotGuard has been deployed. It cites **QoSStress-1** staying within bounds and **SlotGuard traces** meeting deadlines as reasons for conditional adoption. That supports choosing the approach subject to certification; it does not add a deployment claim.
Would certification make every possible control arrival admissible?

No. Certification would justify using the relevant timing bounds in admission; it would not erase SlotGuard's control-admission condition or make unlimited arriving work meet a **2-ms** deadline. A bound can be certified and a particular arriving job can still fail the admission check.
What if certified limits apply only under certain QoS settings or contention conditions?

Then admission could rely on them only within those certified conditions. The decision requires bounds that actually apply to the work being admitted. It does not specify particular QoS settings or contention restrictions, so we should not claim that a certificate of any stated scope already exists.
Is this decision changing SlotGuard's slot size or deadline?

No. The decision concerns the conditional use of **QoS-isolated tiled kernels** and the requirement for **certified bounds before admission**. It does not state a change to SlotGuard's reservation or to the **2-ms** control deadline.
Can I say the approach is approved because the two tests prove the guarantee?

That would overstate the decision. The accurate phrasing is that the approach is **adopted conditionally** because QoSStress-1 stayed within bounds and the SlotGuard traces met deadlines, **with certified bounds required before admission**. The supporting observations and the pre-admission requirement are both essential to its meaning.
Please put the decision into a compact sentence I can use.

**Conditionally adopt QoS-isolated tiled kernels for SlotGuard:** QoSStress-1 stayed within the timing bounds and SlotGuard traces met deadlines, but require certified execution and interference bounds before admitting work on those assumptions.

I want to plan the implementation of QoS-backed SlotGuard: use certified kernel bounds, admit control work only within the ≤1.36-ms interference-inclusive demand limit, reserve 280-µs FIFO inference slots every 8 ms, and validate it under adversarial arrivals.

What does 'with certified kernel bounds' require at the point of admission?

Is the ≤1.36-ms figure the amount of control execution allowed before memory interference is added?

So a job that arrives is not necessarily a job SlotGuard admits?

How do the inference slots fit into that admission decision?

Does FIFO mean the control jobs have to be scheduled FIFO too?

No. Here **FIFO** describes service of inference work in its reserved slots. The plan does not specify a FIFO order for control jobs or a complete scheduling algorithm for all work. Its stated control-side rule is admission within the interference-inclusive demand limit.
And 8 ms isn't an inference deadline, is it?

No. **Every 8 ms** describes the recurrence of a **280-µs** reserved inference slot. An inference kernel may have FIFO work ahead of it, so the slot period should not be rewritten as a promise that each kernel completes within 8 ms. The relevant goal is starvation-free inference progress under adversarial arrivals.
What role does QoS play in the implementation plan without assuming it solves shared-memory interference automatically?

QoS is the proposed backing for managing shared-memory interference. Its configuration must operate within the declared bounds used by the admission and response arguments. Calling the runtime 'QoS-backed' does not itself establish an interference guarantee; the applicable bounds still need to be certified and respected.
Could we implement the slot schedule first and fill in the certified bounds after admitting work?

The plan calls for **certified kernel bounds** as part of admission. A slot schedule alone would not justify admitting work on an unverified nonpreemptible-execution bound. I want validation to challenge both sides of the design. What should it examine conceptually?

Under adversarial arrivals, validation should examine whether admitted control jobs meet their **2-ms deadlines** while the recurring inference reservation and relevant interference are present. Would passing some adversarial validation runs make certified bounds unnecessary?

How should validation handle control jobs that the admission rule rejects?

Would checking only the control deadlines be enough to validate the plan?

No. The runtime also aims for starvation-free inference progress under adversarial arrivals. A validation that checks only admitted control deadlines could miss an implementation that keeps delaying FIFO inference work. What if inference progresses only when arrivals happen to pause?

That would not address the stated adversarial-arrival requirement. Validation should challenge that distinction without treating a finite run as a universal proof.
Can we say the plan guarantees the 2-ms deadlines as soon as the runtime is implemented?

Not merely from implementation. Does the plan include changing the admission ceiling if adversarial validation is difficult?

I want to make sure the kernel bounds and control-admission limit aren't conflated.

Plan to implement **QoS-backed SlotGuard** using **certified kernel bounds**, **control admission at ≤1.36 ms of interference-inclusive demand**, and **280-µs FIFO inference slots every 8 ms**; then perform **adversarial validation** of admitted controls' **2-ms deadlines** and continued FIFO inference progress. I'd like to explore a partitioned accelerator runtime: dedicate one slice to control work and another to inference, give them guaranteed DRAM bandwidth, and admit control jobs using interference-aware response-time analysis.

That is a proposal for separating accelerator capacity while explicitly accounting for what remains shared. What does 'dedicated' need to mean here? I don't want it to be just a scheduling preference.

It needs to be an enforceable partition for the work assigned to each slice. If inference can take capacity reserved for control whenever it is busy, the control slice is not dedicated in the sense this proposal requires. The proposal does not specify whether the partition is implemented in hardware or by an enforceable runtime mechanism, or how large either slice is.
Would an inference kernel being nonpreemptible cease to matter once there are two slices?

Nonpreemptibility remains a property of the inference kernel. With a strictly enforced dedicated partition, however, a kernel running on the inference slice would not directly occupy the control slice while control work waits for that slice. It could still affect control through shared resources, including DRAM, which is why the bandwidth guarantee and interference-aware response analysis remain necessary.
So this is not a claim that partitioning eliminates all interference?

Correct. Dividing accelerator execution capacity does not automatically divide DRAM or remove every effect of shared-memory contention. The proposal explicitly pairs dedicated slices with **guaranteed DRAM bandwidth** and retains **interference-aware** control admission. Claiming interference had vanished would contradict the need to account for it.
Can guaranteed bandwidth simply be an average rate measured across a long run?

An average rate alone may be insufficient for a 2 ms control response argument. Control could encounter a concentrated period of poor memory service even if a long-run average looks acceptable. The DRAM guarantee used by admission needs timing properties strong enough to bound the interference relevant to a control job's response. This proposal does not specify the numerical guarantee or its enforcement method.
Does the proposal prescribe equal slices or equal DRAM shares?

No. It specifies a **dedicated control slice**, a **dedicated inference slice**, and **guaranteed DRAM bandwidth**, but gives no slice sizes, bandwidth amounts, or equality requirement. Selecting those values would require information not contained in the proposal.
What is admission checking if control already has a dedicated slice?

It checks whether the control work assigned to that slice can meet its response deadline under the declared execution and interference bounds. A dedicated slice does not have unlimited capacity, and its jobs may still experience bounded shared-memory interference. The response-time analysis must cover those effects before a control job is admitted with a 2 ms deadline guarantee.
Could I admit every control arrival just because inference cannot run on the control slice?

No. Separating inference execution does not establish that an arbitrary amount of control work fits within 2 ms. Admission is still necessary to distinguish jobs whose worst-case response can be bounded within the deadline from arrivals for which that guarantee has not been established.
Should the response-time analysis ignore DRAM because we've guaranteed bandwidth?

No. The guarantee provides an assumption the analysis can use; it is not permission to ignore memory effects. The admission test must bound the control response under the guaranteed DRAM service and any remaining permitted interference. The guarantee also has to hold in the conditions under which admitted jobs execute.
What's the difference between guaranteeing bandwidth and guaranteeing a control job finishes by 2 ms?

Guaranteed bandwidth is a resource-service property. A 2 ms response guarantee is a conclusion about a job's full response, which also depends on its execution demand and competition from other admitted control work. Interference-aware response-time analysis connects the resource guarantees and declared bounds to that per-job deadline conclusion; bandwidth alone does not establish it.
Could the inference slice help with starvation-free progress under adversarial arrivals?

It provides a plausible basis: inference has dedicated accelerator capacity rather than depending entirely on gaps in control demand, and guaranteed DRAM bandwidth could protect it from indefinite denial of memory service. But the proposal alone does not specify how inference jobs are served within their slice or establish a starvation-free service bound. Continued inference progress under adversarial arrivals remains a requirement to demonstrate.
Does 'dedicated inference slice' imply every inference job has a fixed completion deadline?

No. Dedication identifies where inference can execute, not a per-job latency guarantee. An inference job might have other inference work ahead of it, and no inference deadline or queueing rule is given here. The stated inference objective is starvation-free progress, not completion within a specified number of milliseconds.
If control arrivals are adversarial, can we still keep the inference slice available?

Under the proposed dedicated partition, admitting more control work would not authorize taking away the inference slice. That is the point of making it dedicated rather than merely opportunistic. Could inference contention for DRAM invalidate the control guarantee even though the compute slices stay separate?

It could if that contention exceeds what the control response analysis allows. The proposal therefore requires guaranteed DRAM bandwidth and interference-aware admission: control's worst-case response must be calculated under the memory-service conditions that can actually be enforced while inference uses its slice. A nominal compute partition without an adequate memory guarantee would not by itself justify the 2 ms claim.
Would it be reasonable to call the DRAM guarantee a complete isolation guarantee?

Not on the information provided. It guarantees bandwidth, but the proposal does not say that every shared resource is isolated or that bandwidth alone bounds every possible delay. The safe description is that DRAM has a guaranteed service property to be incorporated in the interference-aware response-time analysis.
Is the control admission rule about total control demand on its slice, or only the execution time of the newest job?

It must establish a response-time bound for the job being considered in the presence of the admitted control work and permitted interference. Checking only the newest job's isolated execution time would not generally account for competition on the control slice. The proposal does not prescribe a formula or numerical demand ceiling.
What happens conceptually if the response-time bound comes out above 2 ms?

That analysis would not justify admitting the job with the stated 2 ms deadline under those conditions. Admission is a condition for the guarantee, not a promise to accept every arrival. A different valid set of conditions would require its own analysis; this proposal supplies no such alternative.
And if the bound is exactly 2 ms?

What needs to be true of the bandwidth promise for the analysis to rely on it?

Calling bandwidth 'guaranteed' without an applicable bound and enforcement conditions would not make an admission result sound.
Could the bandwidth guarantee for control come at the cost of inference never receiving memory service?

Does this proposal choose a preemption mechanism or require that inference kernels be interruptible?

Would passing a few deadline traces be enough to establish the proposed admission guarantee?

How do I describe this as a proposal, without implying that the slices or bandwidth guarantees already exist?

No. It asks whether contention can remain **bounded** in a way compatible with the 2-ms control deadline.
